name: Hot comb straightening

lead: A hot comb is a metal comb with fine teeth, heated on a stove or electrically, and drawn through sections of coarse or curly hair to press it straight and smooth. People use it for a polished, straight style without a chemical relaxer.

Dermatology research has examined its link to central scalp hair loss. The condition once called hot comb alopecia is now called central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, and studies have found a poor correlation between hot comb use and its onset.

paras: Hair is typically washed and dried, sections are pressed with the heated comb, usually with an oil or pressing product, and styled. Results last until the hair gets wet or humid. Details of heat settings are not covered here.

Combs are often heated above 65 C, so burns are common without care.[2] Dermatology reviews discuss a link with scarring hair loss, but a 1992 study found poor correlation between hot comb use and onset, and the cause of CCCA remains unknown.

chain: Heated metal teeth press hair shafts
Sleek straight style without chemical relaxers
angle.text: The comb heats and flattens each section so coily or curly hair looks straight and smooth. The style holds until the hair is washed or humidity returns.

lead: A hot comb, also called a pressing comb, is a heated metal comb used to straighten moderate to coarse hair, working from the roots; it is heated on a direct heat source or electrically.[1] It lets people with textured hair wear a straight, smooth style, typically lasting until moisture returns.

Heated irons for curling hair were introduced in Paris in 1872 by Francois Marcel Grateau.[1] In the US, hot combs were marketed to African American women from the 1910s, and Walter Sammons of Philadelphia received a patent in 1920, followed by Louisa B. Cason in 1922.[1] Madam C. J. Walker is often credited with inventing the hot comb, but she never claimed to and bought combs from suppliers.[1]

Dermatologists have long discussed a scarring hair loss of the central scalp, once called hot comb alopecia. Lopresti's 1968 report linked it to the practice,[2][3] but a 1992 study found poor correlation between hot comb use and onset and proposed the term follicular degeneration syndrome.[4] The condition is now generally called central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a multifactorial condition of uncertain cause.[5][6]

paras: Parisian Francois Marcel Grateau introduced heated irons in 1872.[1] In the US, Mme. Baum's Hair Emporium in New York advertised a straightening comb in 1912, and several other sellers followed in 1915 and 1916.[1] Sammons filed his patent on April 9, 1920 and it was granted on December 21 of that year; Cason filed in 1921 and was granted in 1922.[1]

Early researchers thought hot petrolatum used with the comb caused chronic follicle inflammation.[1] A review noted disorders such as hot-comb and traction alopecia occur mainly among Black patients and relate to hair structure and care methods.[7] Later work described CCCA as a progressive vertex-centered scarring alopecia most common in women of African descent, with unresolved causes.[5][6] In the 1992 study of ten women, correlation between use and onset was poor.[4] Follicular degeneration syndrome was also described in men not using straightening methods.[8] A survey of 529 African American women examined hair-care practices and risk factors.[9] Current reviews describe genetic and environmental factors.[5][10]

No clinical trials of hot comb styling as an intervention have been published. Observational and histologic studies of CCCA include the 1992 series,[4] a survey of 529 African American women on central hair loss and risk factors,[9] and later reviews of epidemiology and treatment.[10]
